utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Good afternoon. Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. This is case number IT-95-13/1-PT, the Prosecutor Mile Mrksic, Miroslav Radic, and Veselin Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Please make yourself comfortable. Let's start with you, Mr. Mrksic. Before we proceed, I want to make sure that you can follow the proceedings in your own language. Yes, Mr. Mrksic. I want to make sure that you can follow the proceedings in your own language. THE ACCUSED MRKSIC: [Interpretation] Yes, I can, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Radic, same question. THE ACCUSED RADIC: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. Yes, I can follow. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, too. Mr. Sljivancanin, same question. Mr. Sljivancanin is not receiving any interpretation, I take it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter cannot hear Mr. Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can he move and use the other microphone, please. Can you hear interpretation now? Can we have technical assistance, please. THE ACCUSED SLJIVANCANIN: [Interpretation] Yes, everything is all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I just, for formality's sake, I just want to confirm that you are receiving interpretation in your own language. THE ACCUSED SLJIVANCANIN: [Interpretation] Yes, it's all right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you, and good afternoon to you, too. You may sit down. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: My name is Moore, I'm a senior trial attorney. I'm assisted by Ms. Mary Tuma, who sits on my right, Mr. Alex Demirdjian, further on my right, and Ms. Sandra D'Angelo, who's on my left, as case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Moore, and good afternoon to you and your team. Appearances for accused Mrksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. Good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom. Appearing for Mr. Mrksic is attorney-at-law Mr. Miroslav Vasic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, and good afternoon to you, Mr. Vasic. Appearances for accused Radic.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. Good afternoon, all. The accused, Miroslav Radic, will be represented today by co-counsel, Mira Tapuskovic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam, and good afternoon to you. And appearances for accused Veselin Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. Good afternoon to everybody. The defence of Mr. Sljivancanin will be represented by Novak Lukic, and my co-counsel, Mr. Momcilo Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Lukic, and good afternoon to you and Mr. Bulatovic. So, the reasons for this Status Conference, first. This is not just a formality. It's important because the public who will be following these proceedings will know exactly what is a Status Conference and why it is convened at regular intervals before the trial starts. First of all, I'd like to remind everyone that the last Status Conference was held way back on the 12th of May of this year, and this one is being held within the time period established under Rule 65 bis, namely, within the 120 days that are set down and within which periodical Status Conferences need to be held. The purpose of a Status Conference is to organise exchanges between the parties so as to ensure an expeditious preparation for trial. Secondly, to review the status of the accuseds' case and to give an opportunity for the accused to raise issues thereto. And last, but not least, to give an opportunity for each of the accused to raise issues in relation to the mental and/or physical conditions and matters generally related to their state of detention. Upon my instructions, our Senior Legal Officer, Mr. Von Hebel, held a 65 ter meeting this morning, and he has reported to me on the outcome of that meeting. I will be touching on several matters that I'm informed were raised during the meeting as we proceed with this Status Conference. This may or may not be the last Status Conference in these pre-trial proceedings. It was certainly meant to be the last one before the 65 ter meeting that you had this morning. I pretty much expect that there might be the need for a further Status Conference as we go along. I will tell you straight away that it will not be me myself that will preside over that Status Conference, because I had already decided before today that, in the course of this week or early next week, I will be appointing, assigning, Judge Kevin Parker to be a Pre-Trial Judge between now and when the trial begins. I suppose you are already aware that it is most likely that Judge Parker will be the Presiding Judge in the trial. So what will be left over today, I think he will be dealing with. For the benefit of the public, there were some developments after the last Status Conference that I think ought to be made public once more. They are public from the press releases of this Tribunal, but I think I can condense the events in a minute or so and inform the general public on what happened. You know that there was, even at the time of the last Status Conference, a motion pending for referral of this case to the special court -- to another court, anyway, to another court, which would not be this Tribunal. Then, on the 9th of June, while the referral motion to -- was still pending before the special Bench that we have dealing with those matters, on the 9th of June, due to potential difficulties specific to the case, which had not been foreseen at the time of filing the relative motion for referral, and -- the Prosecution filed a motion for withdrawal of that motion, requesting the referral Bench to grant leave to withdraw the motion and request for referral and to order the reinstatement of the case to the appropriate Trial Chamber of the Tribunal. Actually, the case didn't need to be reinstated, because it always belonged to the Trial Chamber of this Tribunal, and it would have ceased to be so had there been a referral or a definitive basis. On the 13th of June, in any case, the Defence for the accused filed a joint response opposing the motion for withdrawal and requesting the indictment to be referred to the authorities of Serbia and Montenegro. On the 10th of June, the Government of Serbia and Montenegro filed a submission requesting that the Prosecution motion be rejected and that the indictment in the present case be referred to its relevant authorities. And subsequently, to be precise, on the 30th of June, the referral Bench granted the motion, Prosecution motion for withdrawal, holding that "for reasons already given, this is not an obvious case for referral, and, in the Bench's view, it would be unjustified and unwise to act on its own initiative to order referral in this particular case, given the complexity of the crimes which have been raised by the submissions and the intensity of feelings generated amongst interested parties by the prospect of referral." This is background information for those who were not aware of it. Obviously, present company excluded. So I'll touch upon the first item on the agenda, real item on the agenda, and that is the Prosecution pre-trial brief and list of witnesses required under Rule 66(A)(ii). Upon reviewing the relative documents, I notice that on the 29th of August of this year, the Prosecution filed its pre-trial brief, including its final list of witnesses, or what was described then as the final list of Prosecution witnesses, and according to which the Prosecution intends to call 88 witnesses, 70 of whom would be produced to give evidence viva voce, and 18, the remaining 18, are purported to become Rule 92 bis witnesses. Of course, that stands to be seen. It's a matter to be decided upon at a later stage. Broadly speaking, the witnesses that the Prosecution intends to bring forward, are proposing, can be comfortably or conveniently divided into six categories. The first category would be of professionals, consisting of one ICTY, one Tribunal expert witness, five witnesses from outside this Tribunal, three international witnesses, and that would make it to nine. In addition, it's being sought that there will be two ICTY investigators and five journalists. So this first category would amount to 16. Then there are civilians, of whom 19 of locals, 11 Vukovar Hospital staff, 11 Vukovar Hospital staff. Then there's a third category, consisting of civilians authorities, namely, five members of the autonomous region of SBWS, two members of other civilian authorities. Then there are 14 members of the JNA 1st Guards Motorised Brigade, four members of the JNA 80th Motorised Brigade, seven JNA officers, three members of the local Serb TO and Serb volunteers, five members of the Croatian National Guard, the ZNG, and, finally, two members of the military judiciary. I don't think I need to address this any further. This is information that you already had. I am just relaying it in open court. Then I come to the use of Rules 89(F) and 92 bis. I notice that the Prosecution has not yet filed any motion for the admission of the statements under Rule 92 bis of the Rules, and in addition, the Prosecution has not yet identified the witnesses for whom it intends to introduce written statements pursuant to Rule 89(F). I know that this was discussed this morning and that there is an undertaking which I now need confirmation of, that the motion for the admission of Rule 92 bis statements will be filed by the Prosecution by the 23rd of September, as communicated to you by Mr. Von Hebel during this morning's meeting. Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour is quite correct that we indicated we would endeavour to file that motion by the 23rd of September. My understanding, however, is there may be a difficulty. Whereas OTP can ensure that investigators go and meet the witnesses and ensure that the signature of agreement of the content is -- that the witness is satisfied that it is the truth, the administration require, apparently, three weeks' notice before they can release any members of the Court staff to accompany the OTP. So while we are in a position to do it, I think that the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Registry, as a matter of precedent, require three weeks' notice. This was not something we were aware of. I suspect Mr. Von Hebel was unaware of it as well. But clearly, that creates a difficulty in respect of the 92 bis motions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Right. I thank you, Mr. Moore. That's a very valid point that you have raised. I saw Mr. Von Hebel nodding, so presumably this is news for him as well. So what I suggest you do is you explore, Mr. Von Hebel, with the Registry, whether, first, this process could be expedited for us to be able to retain the date of the 23rd of September. If that is not possible, please, Mr. Moore, consider this to be one of the leftovers to which I will refer towards the end of this Status Conference today. In other words, if Mr. Von Hebel, interceding -- upon interceding with the Registrar to see if the whole process to be expedited to make it possible to retain the 23rd of September is unsuccessful, then obviously we have to find -- to find a solution, and that would be one of the leftovers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Before we move to leftovers, if we may --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm coming to the leftovers later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Before I get to the leftovers, may I deal with the main course, just initially, that we were hoping to send two investigators, and that will cut down the time level. Therefore, it will require two members from the Registry, not one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Von Hebel, is that news again? Yes. All right. You will handle it. You will then liaise with Mr. Moore. If the period established, the deadline established, needs to be extended, then obviously it will be extended, but it will be a matter which I will classify as leftovers and which will be dealt with separately then by Judge Parker instead of by myself. This is what I meant. All right? Am I clear? All right. Thanks. Does the same apply to -- no it doesn't follow, but what about the Rule 89(F). We'll keep the same deadline for the purpose of that Sub-rule?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I know Mr. Von Hebel will have informed the Court of the Prosecution submissions in relation to this. Our submission is as follows: That we will clearly try and identify what I will call alpha witnesses and bravo witnesses, witnesses that we can perhaps place first. And if, as a direct consequence of the nature of examination by the Bench and/or my learned friends, we perhaps then can use the 89(F) procedure. But may I please place on the record that I reserve my position in relation to making any further submissions in respect of this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I thank you, Mr. Moore. Now let's come to matters of disclosure. First of all, about this matter that I have just brought to an end, namely, the list of witnesses, matters related to the pre-trial brief, are there any comments from the Defence? If there are no comments ...

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. The Defence has no comments in this respect. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vasic. Now we come to disclosure, and I will just go through the information as I have tried to collect it and condense it. I am informed, and please correct me if I'm wrong, that the Prosecution has disclosed all statements for witnesses 1 to 53, except for the redacted statements of five so-called sensitive witnesses, to be disclosed to the Defence later on. I am informed that two witnesses have not given statements to the Prosecution and that, for these witnesses, the Prosecution disclosed the transcript of their prior testimonies in other Tribunal cases. This was disclosed on a CD-ROM, I'm told. But I am also informed that the accused do not have access to this medium at the Detention Unit. I have been given to understand that the parties will be meeting. There will be mutual consultations, with a view to finding a more traditional form of disclosing this material and making it thus available to the accused. Am I correct in this information or not? I see some hesitation on the face of Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The traditional method, of course, is hard copy. We are talking probably somewhere between 10 or 15.000 pages, and that in itself will create difficulties. Might I respectfully submit that, and I suspect the Defence will support this, that perhaps with Your Honour's assistance and guidance, that the issue of compatibility of computers and access to computers be dealt with as a matter of priority? Because if that is dealt with initially, then the disclosure and reading of all material will resolve itself. If we leave it to hard copies, I can definitely see problems not only for the Prosecution but also to the Defence teams and the defendants, when they have to carry that amount of papers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Can someone enlighten me?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sorry about that. Can someone enlighten me on the problem that may exist at the unit, the Detention Unit, when it comes to access to data stored in electronic form, such as CD-ROMs? What's the situation? Because at least from the information that I had in other cases, the only problems that I have encountered are problems arising from the accused's side and not from the administration side. In other words, the facilities are there, and when it's a problem of the accused or the detainee requiring assistance, it is also made available. Sometimes it's ordered by the Trial Chamber, sometimes the commandant himself and/or the Registrar make it available. So on a personal level, having followed other cases, being involved, I don't know what the problem is. Perhaps someone can enlighten me. Why is -- if I may ask, why is access by the accused to these CD-ROMs at the Detention Unit not possible?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, nobody has claimed that the access to CD-ROMs at the Detention Unit is impossible. What is at stake here is that the accused Mrksic currently has no computer through which he can access any CD-ROMs, nor is he trained to use computers. In view of how things transpired in this case, and in view of the insufficient amount of time that we had from the minute when the trial beginning was scheduled, until this Status Conference was held, we had no idea in what form the disclosure would be. It turned out that the disclosure was in the form of CD-ROMs. But in addition to that, we also received a large volume of hard-copy material. Now we are faced with the need to ensure that all of the accused have computers so that they can analyse the material disclosed by the OTP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the time being -- I thank you, Mr. Vasic. Is there anything else you would like to state, you or Mr. Lukic or anyone else? Does your client have a computer available?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. My client does have a computer. I was told by my client that he's able to listen to audio recordings which he receives electronically. But now that we are dealing with these typical technical issues, allow me to say that we have the following problem: If he's listening to an audio recording, and we are talking of very long recordings, he has to listen to the entire version in B/C/S in order to be able to give me instructions. In that sense, it is much easier for us to conduct searches of the English-language material and then to analyse only portions of it. But our clients, even if they are trained in the use of computers, have to listen to the entire length of very long transcripts, which perhaps do not relate to Vukovar alone but may relate to some other issues. And these are very, very long transcripts. Our clients are unable to read the material. They can only listen to the audio recording.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Tapuskovic, do you want to make a statement in this regard or not?

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I would like to add something to what my colleague Lukic stated. When an accused listens to an audio recording of a trial, when he listens at the DU to a testimony given by a witness, the time is seen on the screen. If the accused wishes to give any kind of instruction to his Defence counsel, the accused has to say, at such-and-such time, at such-and-such hour, such-and-such minute, the witness said the following. We have no technical capabilities to find that exact portion in the material that we receive, in the form that we receive it. This problem arose when a large amount of transcripts was disclosed, as my colleague, my learned friend Mr. Moore said, that was the material which was between 10.000 and 15.000 pages. The disclosure was completed. However, the technical facilities are not adequate in order to enable the accused to have proper access to this material and to ensure that their rights are respected in this sense. This is a very serious technical issue. Other technical issues and problems that we are faced with have to do with whether the computer is purchased by the Registry or by the family of the accused. If the family of the accused has to procure a computer, then this computer is, so to speak, confiscated by the Registry for quite a long period of time in order to check it thoroughly. And unfortunately, right now, when the beginning of the trial is so close, we don't have the luxury of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I take it, because we have digressed a little and touched upon other matters that are related but which I did not have in mind to deal with today. As I take it, the problem as it arose related only to the two witnesses that had not given statements to the Prosecution. And the Prosecution decided to disclose the transcripts of their prior testimonies in other cases on CD-ROM. Could we, at least as far as the testimony, the transcript of the testimony of these two witnesses, provide the parties with a hard copy? Now, and this, we're certainly talking about thousands here. Without creating a precedent or without prejudicing your position as regards electronic disclosure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: If we can provide it, we'll do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's leave it at that, because basically what I had been reported was in relation to this. On the other hand, if, as we go along, or as you go along, we will need to refer to CD-ROMs that have been disclosed, and of course I acknowledge that you will need continuous consultation with your clients and that your clients must have access to these CD-ROMs, I see problems if at least one of them -- I take, Mr. Vasic, Mr. Mrksic, your client, hasn't even got at his disposal a computer at the moment. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, as I've said, Your Honour. It's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So has this been discussed between you or your client and the Registry -- and the Registrar? Has this matter come up for discussion?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this matter was not raised. The disclosure was received -- the largest portion of the material that was disclosed to us was received within the last two weeks, when we were very busy working on our pre-trial brief. Therefore, we had no time to react. In addition to that, we also have the problems that my colleagues, the other Defence counsel, informed you about, concerning the material disclosed to us by the OTP. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What I want to find out for the time being is if there is a problem in providing your client with a PC, with a personal computer, or whatever kind of computer is necessary. Has he filed a demand for one, a claim for one, or not yet? Because if he's filed a claim for one and it's been refused, it's one thing. If the matter hasn't come up before the Registrar, it's completely another matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This matter was not raised before the Registry. My client will request a computer. The matter was not raised earlier because the pace of disclosure and the pace of motions submitted by the OTP was such that he had no time to demand this earlier. My client will put in a request and we will inform the Chamber about the outcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm going to inform Judge Parker that this may become an outstanding matter later on which he might decide he needs to deal with. So Mr. Sljivancanin has a computer. Is it his own or was it provided to him by the Registry?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think he has his own computer which he received from his family. But another issue, Your Honour, that I need to raise for the record. We are not referring to the transcripts of only two witnesses. We received at least -- we received transcripts of at least 15 witnesses within the past few weeks.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to add something else. We are very grateful for your willingness to see that this matter is resolved. As we are talking about a very large number of CDs. Only one witness gave interview for 11 days, and this material is on seven CDs. Therefore, you see what amount of material this is, how much time is needed in order to analyse this, to go over this with our clients. The testimony of certain individuals or certain statements that were, for example, given in the Milosevic case, were given over a very long period of time. So not all of the transcripts pertain to our indictment specifically. However, it is much easier for us, as Defence counsel, to analyse an issue much quicker than our clients. We are not always present here; therefore, we cannot keep on working at it with our clients. Now, another matter that I would like to raise, and I pray for understanding, both from the Chamber and from the OTP, is this: When I brought some CDs to my client, Mr. Vasic [as interpreted], they were almost confiscated from me because they were not labelled with the text indicating that these CDs were the property of the OTP. Because the DU believes that any of us can take any CD-ROM and put a label on it. What we need to do is that we need to ensure that the CDs are properly labelled. Otherwise, the officials at the Detention Unit will confiscate the material in order to verify whether this was the material that was properly disclosed by the OTP. We understand the safety issues and other regulations in place of the Detention Unit; however, they seriously impede the work that has to be done in order to prepare for the case with your clients.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Your client's computer, is it his own or was it provided to him by the ...

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Radic has his own personal computer, and he is much more trained to use it than I am, to tell you the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let me make myself understood also, that when I said Mr. Mrksic to maybe proceed with filing a claim, I am in no way committing the Tribunal with a responsibility or a duty to provide him with one. And there's a policy, of course, which is followed, and I would not interfere with that. Similarly, I wouldn't interfere, Madam Tapuskovic, and please do understand me, with the protocol that is resorted to, was established and observed at the Detention Unit. If they have their own requirements for reasons that they believe are necessary, be it security, be it others, I would be the last one to interfere with those. So if there are rules as to how they should be labelled and how they should be made available, et cetera, please try to make sure that the rules are followed. Don't expect any of the Judges to intervene in matters that are beyond their jurisdiction and belong exclusively to the commandant of the Detention Unit who, I must state publicly, is very much aware of the rights of each of the detainees and tries to ensure that there is no obstruction when it comes to the consultations that they need to have with Defence counsel. So I wouldn't intervene for the time being, because I don't see why I should intervene.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I deeply regret if you took my words as a request for any kind of intervention on your part. No, that was not my intention. The Defence is absolutely willing to adhere to any rules in place at the Detention Unit. I simply wanted to explain the kind of problems we're facing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think these problems are arising on a daily basis, actually. Not in this case only, but in every other case. Now, I am informed that the English versions of witnesses 54 to 84 were disclosed to the Defence on the 29th of July, and the B/C/S version of the same was disclosed on the 19th of August. If that information is not correct, please correct it now. I'm also informed by Mr. Von Hebel that this morning he directed the Prosecution to file a motion requesting protective measures for the remaining witnesses on Monday, this Monday, coming Monday, or soon thereafter. Again, please register any disagreement with what I'm stating now if my statement is not correct. Yes, Ms. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I must say that Defence teams have an ongoing, almost permanent contact with the OTP, in order to ensure that we inform the Chamber in the most accurate way about what has been disclosed. At the 65 ter meetings, between those meetings, and during Status Conferences, we regularly meet in order to compare our data. Most likely because of a very short period of time that elapsed between the last meeting and this one, a misunderstanding arose because of that. And in the meantime, some issues, some things changed, and perhaps this is what caused the confusion. Five witnesses were granted protective measures in March of this year. Their statements have finally been disclosed to us in their unredacted version. That was done today. As you can see, Your Honour, based on the list of witnesses dated the 29th of August, there are some new witnesses on that list for whom protective measures will be sought, mostly witnesses from Witness 20 and on, because the list of witness 1 to 19 is identical to the previous lists. Out of that number, there remain six statements, or six witnesses, concerning which we have no information. We have neither B/C/S nor English version of their statements. As we were just told by the OTP, they wish to submit a new motion for new protective measures. Based on our records, there is another one, or perhaps two witnesses, who have no protective measures granted and whose identity is known to us, in relation to whom we received no statements, be it in B/C/S or in English. With your leave, we would like now to discuss some issues related to future protective measures. As you may be well aware, Your Honour, a large number of witnesses scheduled to testify here already testified in previous cases, namely, the Dokmanovic and Milosevic trials. The witnesses sought protective measures, and, in the order dated the 9th of March this year, there were two groups of witnesses from two OTP motions for protective measures. The Defence never once objected to protective measures being granted to witnesses who testified previously in the Dokmanovic and Milosevic case under protective measures. We objected only in those instances where the witnesses gave previous testimonies, be it here or in national courts, without any protective measures. The Chamber granted our requests in such instances, and in two cases refused to grant protective measures to two witnesses, P4 and P14. When the time comes for the Defence to respond to the OTP requests, it is much easier for the Defence to do it before the Chamber rules on it, because it is much easier to object before the Chamber rules on it. Therefore, if you believe that it is justified in this case, we would like to ask the OTP to state whether the witness seeking protective measures already testified in a previous case, perhaps Dokmanovic or Milosevic case, or in another case - very important both for the OTP and for us - that we normally refer to as the Ovcara case. I think this is a very important issue. Today we received statements of witnesses with protective measures, and it is our understanding that these witnesses previously testified, both here and in Belgrade, without protective measures. No justification was given in the OTP motion, at least not in the motion we received. Perhaps the OTP put the justification or the reasons for protective measures in their ex parte motion that we never saw. But we would like to kindly ask the OTP to always put in a justification for such a request in all of their future motions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- issue straight away a fact that a person may have given evidence here or else where without any protective measures in place in the past does not necessarily mean that under all circumstances, by all means, he must or she must be refused any protective measures before this Tribunal now. Because circumstances may have changed. What's certain is that the practice, at least to my knowledge, has always been that if the Prosecution is seeking protective measures for particular prospective witness, reasons are given. And if there are no reasons or if the reasons given are insufficient, then the consequence is that the Trial Chamber will not grant the protective measures being sought. So I would leave it -- I do not -- I cannot tell the Prosecution what they should or should not include in their respective motions, because I suppose they know that if the reasons brought forward are not sufficient, they will not be successful in the motion. Secondly, I do think that it would be important for the Trial Chamber at least to know if the person on whose behalf the Prosecution is seeking protective measures has given evidence, testimony, in other trials here, or elsewhere, and whether such evidence was given with protective measures in place, I think that would be very useful information. I will not impose it, of course, on the Prosecution, because I don't think it's the case of imposing it at this particular stage. But I think it would be extremely useful information that would enable the Trial Chamber, whatever the composition, to be able to come to a good decision. I think I've sent my message loud and clear, without making any positions which I think would be out of place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: No. We would agree with that particular assessment. It's clearly a factor for the Court to take into account, but not definitive, and we will assist the Court in that respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, and I appreciate that, Mr. Moore. And thank you, Ms. Tapuskovic, for raising the matter. Now, the other thing I wanted to clear, because I feel I have a little bit of confusion in my mind now, is I'm going to ask you a simple question. Are there any witnesses the identity of whom is still unknown to the Defence, or are you now fully aware of the identity of all the witnesses, including those that you were unaware of until recently?

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will continue, Your Honour, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. because this is an issue that has been delegated to me by my colleagues. We have several more witnesses for whom protective measures will be sought, from P022 to P028. The total number of witnesses who already have protective measures or will be granted them, is 29, according to the current list of the OTP. However, the identity of Witnesses P22 to P28 is still not disclosed to us, has not been disclosed to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you agree to that, Mr. Moore? Yes, Ms. Tuma.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Yes. When it comes to the witnesses number P22 and P28, it is correct that those statements have not yet or the identity has not yet been disclosed to the Defence, due to there are highly sensitive witnesses in another case in this Tribunal. And the Prosecution is -- will file a motion, an urgent motion, concerning protective measures in that respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And out of the five, original five sensitive witnesses, the delayed disclosure of identity of whom was by our decision of the 9th of March 2005 delayed to 30 days prior to the start of the trial, what's the position about those?

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: They were supposed to have been disclosed by the 3rd of September.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Those five sensitive witness statements have been disclosed to the Defence today. And the unredacted statements of those five sensitive witnesses have been disclosed earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: So that is done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So that makes it clear, because the confusion in my mind arose out of the statement that you made earlier on, which gave me the impression that there was nothing pending in this area. All right. When do you intend to file this urgent motion for protective measures?

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We have been in discussion with the Senior Legal Officer earlier on this question, and a date of 15 September has been agreed upon. That is next Wednesday, next week, next Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you live with that, members of the Defence teams? If there is an opposition, please rise. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether there is a misunderstanding. Either you misunderstood us or we misunderstood you, Your Honour. The issue is that the identity of six witnesses, at this point in time, is still not familiar to us. So this is what my colleague was saying. And as for the rest, the sooner we receive material from the OTP, the better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is absolutely no misunderstanding. In fact, the only confusion as I said that arose in my mind, because from one side I was being given the impression that this matter was still outstanding; on the other hand, I heard Ms. Tapuskovic saying that this morning, or today, the names had been disclosed, et cetera. And so I said: Is it pending or not pending any further? But obviously there is an explanation. We're talking of two categories of people here. So I will not impose a deadline. Once you seem to be committed with yourself to file the relative motion by the 15th. However, please, this will need to be monitored by staff. And if there is no filing by the 15th, I am to be informed, Mr. Von Hebel. Thank you. Yes. Other disclosure matters. I'll deal first with expert witnesses' reports. I'm told that five -- as I said earlier, five expert witnesses will give evidence for the Prosecution. Three expert reports have been disclosed to the Defence. For the two remaining experts, the English version of the reports, I'm told, will be disclosed on the 10th of September. And the B/C/S version will be disclosed later, but as soon as possible. Do you confirm this? I'm also told, before you confirm it, Mr. Moore, that your team is facing problems with regard to the translation of one of the expert reports, namely, that of Mr. Theunens, due to its voluminous size, and that during this morning's meeting, you - I mean the Prosecution - declared that it would be in a position to provide more detail as to when the translation is to be expected. I don't know if you've had time to think about it and update us in this respect, but perhaps you can deal with this matter of the expert reports, what's outstanding from it, now, if you wish so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Dealing with Mr. Theunens, whose report has concluded in first draft, and I anticipate will not require any amendment, he is in the nicest possible way, rather loquacious, and therefore it requires further consideration. The interpretation of it and the translation, I've tried to ascertain exactly when that will be done. We can give the English copies at the start of next week, but I'm not able to definitely say when the translations will be done. All I know is, and I hope the Court will accept my undertaking that I will provide the translation as soon as I possibly can, and I know I will be having it marked as urgent, or priority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What's the subject matter of his expertise?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It's command and control in relation to the JNA function and general army matters and it really relates to the core of the case because this is a military case, in substance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It definitely needs to be made available in B/C/S to the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It does, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I haven't quite finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: That's all right. The second relates to General Pringle. That statement is a much shorter statement. The translation for that can be done fairly quickly, and I anticipate and I hope that it will be finished by way of translation by the end of next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Moore. I've taken note of that. And Judge Parker will intervene in this matter, if needed, in due course, if there is an undue delay or unexpected delay in making available the B/C/S version of Mr. Theunens's expert report. Yes. Then I'm told there is material from the Dokmanovic proceedings, which has been provided to the Defence in the English language. If that is not correct information that I have, please tell me. And that the material from the Milosevic, Slobodan Milosevic proceedings, disclosure is still ongoing, as is the case. All right. Yes, Ms. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, your conclusion is correct. This is a protracted case. The Defence, working simultaneously on the pre-trial brief, is searching the Milosevic transcripts on its own, because this has been published on the Tribunal website. We will draw up a list of material we are interested in, which the OTP perhaps will not disclose to us, so that we will request for certain transcripts to be disclosed. For the most part, these are testimonies given in closed session. But we conclude from the previous parts of what these witnesses say that they refer to Vukovar, or the subject matter of this indictment. In our estimation, this will amount to 8.500 to 9.000 pages of transcript, and of course this will require work on the part of both the Defence and the Prosecution, because we don't know whether the entire testimony of these witnesses refers to this indictment or not. But this will require a lot of work, covering a long time, both on the part of the Prosecution and the Defence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Ms. Tapuskovic, and I realise that. And there is also the question of exhibit lists, which arises from the pre-trial documents, brief and accompanying documents that have been filed. For your information, it seems that the Prosecution has filed its list of exhibits on the 29th of August, and although the current list contains a proposed 846 exhibits, the Prosecution has stated that it will continue to review its list to reduce it as much as possible. As it stands, the exhibit list is divided into five parts. I don't need to go into this. And I understand that this is a commitment on your part. I also do understand that exhibits come to the surface as the case unfolds and continue to arrive and surface practically until the end of each case here. So that is understandable. But please do try to keep the exhibits, the number of exhibits, to what is essential, but to the bare minimum, as much as possible. I come to Rule 68 disclosure. I would like you to confirm that, as of last Friday, 2nd of September, the Prosecution had forwarded 29 batches of disclosed material, including B/C/S versions of the Ovcara, of the Belgrade proceedings. The English version of three transcripts from the Belgrade proceedings was disclosed to the Defence, I'm told, on the 1st September. If you disagree with this statement, please speak out now. I am also told that, by my Senior Legal Officer, that the Prosecution has informed him that they have run an ISU search as regards the first 43 witnesses and have disclosed 40 documents, pursuant to Rule 68, and that the Prosecution now is in the process of reviewing the search for the remaining witnesses, basically of Witnesses 44 to 84, and will in due course disclose any documents that might surface pursuant to Rule 68. I am also happy to notice that the Prosecution made it clear to Mr. Von Hebel, in the presence of the three Defence teams this morning, that the ISU search that I mentioned already, for the purposes of Rule 68, is being given the highest priority by the Prosecution. I appreciate that. That's how it should be, and I thank you for it, Mr. Moore, and your team. I also wish to make it clear that this is also in your best interest, because there may be consequences, as you know, with the possibility or ability to call witnesses for whom Rule 68 disclosure has not been concluded. I'm sure you are as aware of this consequence as I am, and I do not, of course, blame you for giving the matter your highest priority. But I do appreciate the fact that you have acknowledged it and that you have made it clear to our Senior Legal Officer. Duration of the trial. I've discussed also this matter with Judge Parker before I started this Status Conference, also because it's of more concern to him than it is to me. We've made our calculations, basically on the basis of 88 witnesses, of whom 18 possibly could have their testimony produced pursuant to Rule 92 bis. We have an indication that the viva voce witnesses are expected to be examined in roughly 250 hours. I'm not going to deal with how many hours are required to examine the Rule 92 bis witnesses. More or less according to the calculations that we have made, my staff and I, and also in consultation with Judge Parker, we're talking of 25 weeks for the Prosecution case to be heard. That would be approximately 125 days. I do encourage you to make your own calculations, and, if my calculations are wrong, to come forward and tell me so. You will recall, those of you who were here present during the last Status Conference, that I tried to impress with you the importance that I attach to the procedure of resorting to agreed facts in -- Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. pursuant -- sole purpose, pursuant to paragraph H of Rule 65 ter. I do notice that, from the information that Mr. Von Hebel has given me, that there is going to be some kind of consultation soon between the parties on this matter, and that the Prosecution has presented a new list of 12 additional facts to the Defence, that the Defence has provided its common position on last Friday, and that you will continue meeting on this topic, and hopefully to come -- bring your discussions to some good fruition before the trial starts. I mean, I'm not going to address it any further, because I have no reason to think that you will not do this. Then, when I thought I had everything prepared for this Status Conference last week, I find on my desk a motion from Mr. Vasic, on behalf of Mrksic. Mr. Vasic, in his motion, expresses the difficulties that he is facing with regard to the appointment of co-counsel and states that he intended to appeal the decision of the Registrar, who refused the proposed co-counsel. I verified that Defence counsel indeed filed its defence motion. This motion was filed on the 2nd of September. And the Trial Chamber is being requested to allow the assignment of Mr. Goran Rodic as co-counsel for his client. Our position is that we are still awaiting for some information to be forthcoming from the Registrar. As I told you before, I will pretty soon be assigning -- passing on my responsibilities as Pre-Trial Judge to Judge Parker, and I think, Mr. Vasic, rather than dwelling on this matter any further, I will just inform you that this is one of the matters that will be dealt with by my successor. But I can also assure you that we are already giving it the -- our utmost attention. Start of the trial. And this is again one area where I thought I was coming to you without any problems, and now seeing the date more or less when the trial would have started. And I recognise that after this morning's meeting, we will need to put a little bit of thought, dedicate a little bit of thought to this matter. I will try to explain as much as possible. But again, it will be Judge Parker who will be dealing with this in due course. I have explained also to him that I will try to hand to him as clean a slate as possible, and that is what I am effectively trying to do. You will recall that the Prosecution -- I told you that the Prosecution filed its pre-trial brief on the 29th of August. On the 31st of August, the Pre-Trial Judge, that's me, granted the joint Defence request for extension of time in which to file their pre-trial brief, and I extended it to the 23rd of September, 2005. The idea is to -- or was until recently - we'll have to see whether we'll stick to this or not, but probably we'll have to delay a little bit the start of the trial. It depends on what Judge Parker will decide. The idea was to have a Pre-Trial Conference on Monday, the 3rd of October, and then we will start with the opening statements immediately after and the case proper in as far as presentation of evidence would have started on the 11th of October, 2005. These were the preparations that I had put in place, also in conformity with the promise I had made to your clients a long time ago that I would do my utmost to ensure that this case comes to trial as soon as possible. I thought that all my problems for the day had finished until I met Mr. Von Hebel this morning after he had finished with the 65 ter meeting, and he informed me that there were some problems that were encountered and that there was a proposition on the part of the Defence, following positions taken by the Prosecution, and outstanding matters, that -- namely, that the Defence would be seeking for the start, the commencement of the trial to be delayed by four or five weeks. I have discussed this with Judge Parker, who is a member of my Trial Chamber and who will, as I said, be the Presiding Judge in the trial. Of course, at the present moment, this remains pending. What I am going to do is that I'm going to fix a time-limit for the Defence teams to file a joint motion, the relative joint motion, and of course at the same time fix a time-limit for the Prosecution response. I'm going to give the Defence team a week from today, hoping that does not create any undue problems to you. And the Prosecution will have ten days from today within which to file a response. I am not giving you the same amount of time, Mr. Moore, for the simple reason that more or less you are already aware of what the problem is and what the reasons are. It's only that the matter will be now dealt with adequately by my successor. I don't think it's really appropriate for me to deal with it myself, when he will be the person who will preside over the trial. So that's the position. I see -- I recognise Mr. Lukic. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. On behalf of all three Defence teams, I have to say a few words to explain why this topic was raised today. I will not burden the record or Your Honour, because I feel that at today's 65 ter meeting, both sides presented a number of problems. But I do have to mention something that is important for our clients and us professionally. We, as the Defence, are not to blame for the position we are in now, and this is well known through all the previous 65 ter Conferences and 11 bis proceedings. Today we are divided between two fundamental rights of the accused: The right from 21(4)(b) and the right to have an expeditious trial without undue delay. Our clients have instructed us that they want the proceedings to begin as soon as possible. It is, however, our professional duty to ensure that we carry out our task in a professional manner and be well prepared for the trial. Therefore, we ask you, as the Pre-Trial Judge and the future Presiding Judge, to bear in mind the specific nature of this case. This case deals with an event which occurred over a period of just a few days. About a year before we found about 250 different testimonies in various cases. And unless we are fully familiar with all the statements and testimonies in advance, we will not be able to cross-examine effectively. And this is the only reason, as we will state in our written submission, that we request a delay. When we had the 11 bis hearing, we said we were ready for the start of the trial, but only now have we received the position of the OTP in their brief, and we really have to prepare thoroughly and ensure that our clients have a really fair trial, as guaranteed by all the rules and regulations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, by all means, Mr. Lukic, and at no time, of course, was I even thinking of hinting that any possible delay that might be attributable to you. When I say "you," to your clients or their counsel. What I would like to stress with you and impress with you is just one thing: Make sure that, any motion, you explain the new circumstances that, according to you, may have arisen, and the predicament in which you contend that you find yourselves in, and then it will, of course, be up to Judge Parker to decide, maybe in consultation also with the other two Judges of the Trial Chamber, pre-Trial Chamber, what will happen. I will leave this matter open and it will be dealt with adequately. And I can assure you reasonably after that your motion and the Prosecution response have been filed. Is there any other matter that you would like to raise? I start with the Prosecution, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, there is one topic. It's called e-court, which I'm sure Your Honour is absolutely delighted to deal with at this time. We would like to know whether, in actual fact, e-court is a feasible option in this case. Because clearly, it requires a different type of preparation. Mr. Von Hebel has been extremely helpful about it, but we still are no further to understanding exactly what the decision will be. What I'm worried about is that suddenly, and I don't mean this in any unkind or pejorative way, a decision will be made that there will be e-court, and we have -- already have timed in our preparations for the normal trial and then there are additional timing constraints which may affect the trial as a whole. And may use an English phrase in saying now it's time to grasp the nettle, to say whether, in actual fact, there is going to be e-court here or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, I think it's a matter that needs to be decided, not only with regard to this case, but generally speaking. And I think you know, as much as I do, that it is being discussed at the moment. And a decision is in the offing. There are quite a few considerations to be taken and there have been consultations going on, but until there is a decision taken at a higher level that e-court will be implemented, I cannot make an open declaration here in open court that it will be implemented in this case. And even so, it might not be implemented in the full extent or fashion that it has been presented; there may be some changes to it. Again, I don't think I can safely tread on that ground now. If there is an adoption of the system, and it will be put in place also with regard to this case, as one would expect it to be, and if that causes you or, for that matter, and probably more so, the Defence, some time constraints, but initially certainly with the Prosecution, then you ought to bring that to the attention of my successor, because I think it's a very important consideration that needs to be taken before we jump to the conclusion that the trial will definitely start on such-and-such a date. I can't tell you more than that, unfortunately, Mr. Moore, because I'm not in a position to confirm anything beyond what I have stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Might I just make one final submission to Your Honour? I had the dubious pleasure of doing a case in London with e-court facilities. It certainly moves the case on, as far as I remember. I've heard the figure 10 or 15 per cent. But as I say, all I want to do on behalf of OTP is to know exactly what it is we're facing, and we really do need answers from someone as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but I think a decision on e-court will be taken very shortly, probably -- I wouldn't even dare end that-- add days. But it's in the offing, anyway. It's in the offing. But I cannot anticipate what the decision will be or whether the project itself will be maintained as it is in its entirety or whether it will be subject to some changes. Any matters that you would like to raise on the part of the Defence? None. So let's come to the other very important part of the Status Conference. Mr. Mrksic, you heard me state in the beginning of this Status Conference that one of the reasons for summoning or convening such Status Conferences is to see what the situation is as regards your state of detention, whether you have -- you wish to communicate to me anything in relation to your health or any other problems that you may encounter which would require my intervention. THE ACCUSED MRKSIC: [Interpretation] I have been here for three and a half years. I can see that you are familiar with my health. I've had heart problems, as you are aware. My health improved here. I don't know whether it is due to the food or the daily routine at the Detention Unit. But, at any rate, it has improved. Now I can tell you, after having listened to this Status Conference and having listened to Status Conferences of the past three and a half years, it reminded me of a saying that we have that the army is waiting for a chance to run and then runs awaiting something else. You said that this was a military case. And I've had a lot of time so far to study the case, but I was unable to do that. I don't have a computer, and I am a man of advanced age. And in my time, we did not use computers very much. Now, in a situation where I have fairly fragile health, and where I have to work very hard in order to go through a large amount of material looking for important bits and pieces, this is something that will fully adversely affect my health. In addition to that, we're now rushing to begin the trial. We want to begin the trial as soon as possible. However, I'm afraid that -- what's going to happen with it. And now you're mentioning this e-court. I'm absolutely unaware of that system. Perhaps that would endanger our right to have a fair trial or to have a trial at all. I hope that the time that is left can be used in a positive way so that we are indeed prepared once the trial begins. As it stands now, we still do not know who the witnesses are going to be, and this is something that deeply concerns me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Mrksic. I'm sure that Mr. Vasic will assist you in all that you need, and I can assure you that certainly any system adopted here for trial purposes will not be one that will curtail on your rights. It will rather enhance your due process, rights, and those of a fair trial. So you needn't worry about that. There are others, particularly the Judges, that will make sure that the trial that you will receive will be a fair one, in the tradition of this Tribunal. Mr. Radic. THE ACCUSED RADIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you for granting me the opportunity to speak. As far as my health is concerned, everything is fine. In addition to that, I have no other complaints concerning the conditions at the Detention Unit. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Radic. And Mr. Sljivancanin. THE ACCUSED SLJIVANCANIN: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. President, I have neither questions nor complaints, and I ask that the trial begin as scheduled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Thank you. So that brings to an end the Status Conference for today. We stand adjourned. And if there is need for a further Status Conference, it will be held, as I said, by Judge Parker and not by me. So as far as this case is concerned, I don't think you will see my face again. Thank you.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the Status Conference adjourned at
